{{pagebanner|Iztacalco CDMX banner.jpg}}

'''Iztacalco''' is a borough of [[Mexico City]]. It is a mostly residential, densely populated, working-class borough (''alcaldia'' in CDMX-lingo), in the eastern-central part of Mexico City (CDMX). Many visitors coming to the city for major sporting events or music festivals find themselves in Iztacalco without realizing that it's where the ''Ciudad Deportivo'' (including the Hermanos Rodriguez motorsports complex) is located. Almost all foreign tourists will pass through at least a portion of the borough because it's also the part of the city that's home to the [[Benito Juárez International Airport]]. Most foreigners don't do much sightseeing in the borough, but if they did, they'd find pre-Hispanic and colonial historical sights along with some great street food experiences and an extremely authentic local cultural experience. Iztacalco is best experienced by a street-savvy visitor who speaks Spanish well. It is generally not a good neighborhood for casual strolls or "explorations".
[[File:MonasteryareaMatiasIzta.jpg|thumb|San Matias monastery in Iztacalco]]

==Get in==
{{mapframe}}
Iztacalco is easy to reach via public transportation. It is only about 5 km east of the [[Mexico City/Centro|Centro Historico]],  but is not a walkable route because of the many busy roads and highways you would have to cross. An Uber or taxi can get there in 15 minutes or less if the traffic isn't bad but it can also take 90 minutes or more during rush hour. Metro is usually the best option and there are several stations in Iztacalco.

==Connect==
5G wireless is available throughout the neighborhood. Telcel is the major carrier. The CDMX government provides free WiFi access in parks and public spaces. 

== Stay safe ==
While most of the neighborhood consists of working-class families going about their daily routine, certain pockets have higher crime rates. The area is regularly patrolled by CDMX police, but this is not a tourist area and has none of the extra patrols or police units that are specifically trained in dealing with tourists. It is not a particularly dangerous area but is best approached with caution by a street-savvy visitor with good Spanish language skills. If you decide to visit, take normal precautions like leaving your credits cards and ID in your hotel safe, dressing down in casual, discreet clothes, and traveling during daylight in a group (preferably accompanied by a local guide who will help guide you to interesting spots while avoiding potential trouble spots.
